ἔργων προφητείαν ἀλληγορίαν ὠνόμασεν. Gal 4,25 Οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἐμνημόνευσε τοῦ Σινᾶ ὄρους, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ οἱ Ἀγαρηνοὶ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰσμαὴλ τὴν ἔρημον ἔχουσι τὴν παρατείνουσαν ἕως τοῦ Σινᾶ ὄρους. ἐν δὲ τῷ Σινᾷ ὁ νόμος ἐδόθη εἰς δουλείαν γεννῶν, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ Σινᾶ ὄρους αἱ πλάκες δοθεῖσαι ἐκομίσθησαν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ, καὶ πολλάκις μετενεχθεῖσαι ἀπὸ τόπου εἰς τόπον τελευταῖον ἱδρύθησαν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις. διὰ τοῦτο ἐπήγαγεν· συστοιχεῖ δὲ τῇ νῦν Ἱερουσαλήμ, δουλεύει δὲ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς. ὅπου γῆς ἐπαγγελία, καὶ κτῆσις καὶ γάμος καὶ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, καὶ δουλεία ἀκολουθεῖ· ὅπου δὲ ἀπαλλαγὴ τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς φροντίδων καὶ τῶν δεσμῶν, καὶ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἡ πολιτεία, ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς πολιτείας ἡ ἐλευθερία. Gal 5,17 Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας. ἐπειδὴ τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν ὁ νόμος, διὰ δὲ τούτου διερεθίζεται ἡ ἐπιθυμία καὶ ἀκατάσχετος οὖσα πρὸς ἁμαρτίαν ἄγει. τούτου ἕνεκεν ὅτε νόμου ἦν μνήμη, μέμνηται καὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους τοῦ νόμου μνημονεύων καὶ τῆς διὰ τοῦ κυρίου διορθώσεως εἰσήγαγεν, τὸ οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶντες θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται. διὰ τί δὲ συνεχωρήθη τὸ τρυφᾶν καὶ ἐσθίειν; ὅτι ἡ τῶν ὡμολογημένων κακῶν ἀποχὴ οὐκ ἂν προεχώρησεν, εἰ μὴ ἐνεδόθη αὐτοῖς τὸ ἐσθίειν 304 καὶ πίνειν· ᾔδει μὲν γὰρ ὁ νομοθέτης ὅτι ἀδύνατον τρυφῶντας κρατεῖν ἡδονῶν. τέως δὲ ἠθέλησε τὸν νοῦν παιδεῦσαι, ἵνα γνῷ τί καλὸν καὶ τί κακὸν καὶ τί τὸ εὐσεβές· προεώρα γὰρ ὅτι ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι ὁ τὸ λεῖπον τῷ νόμῳ προστιθείς, λέγω δὴ τὸ μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατεῖν, ὡς λέγει ὁ Παῦλος. Gal 6,7–8 Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελευομένοις, τοῖς δὲ τὴν Παύλου διδασκαλίαν κηρύττουσιν οὐδὲν παρεῖχον. διό φησιν· ὁ σπείρων εἰς τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ· ὁ γὰρ νόμῳ ὑποκείμενος ἐν τοῖς σαρκικοῖς ζῇ. ὁ τοίνυν τῷ ταῦτα διδάσκοντι παρέχων εἰς τὴν σάρκα σπείρει μόνον. Gal 6,14–15 Ἵνα μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκροβυστίας ἀντιποιεῖσθαι, καὶ οὐχὶ περιτομῆς καὶ διαβολῆς πρόφασιν δῷ τοῖς ἀντιλέγουσιν, κάλλιστα ἐπήγαγε τὸ τελευταῖον, ὅτι οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει οὔτε ἀκροβυστία, καινὴν δὲ κτίσιν εἶπεν. περὶ ἧς ἀλλαχοῦ· εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις. εἰ καινή, φησί, κτίσις, μὴ γίνου ὑπὸ νόμον· ὁ γὰρ ζῶν κατὰ νόμον ἐν κόσμῳ ζῇ, ὁ δὲ ζῶν ἐν Χριστῷ, ἐν οὐρανοῖς πολιτεύεται. ἐσταύρωται οὖν ἐμοὶ κόσμος κἀγὼ κόσμῳ.
thought_title: Allegory as enacted prophecy; why Paul mentions sin with the law; sowing to the flesh; only the new creation matters
orientation: Eusebius is closing his commentary on Galatians, explaining Paul's final remarks about Sinai, the law and sin, sowing to the flesh, and the new creation.
pass_a_gloss: Now therefore he called the prophecy through deeds an allegory. He did not mention Mount Sinai simply, but because the Hagarenes, those from Ishmael, hold the desert that stretches as far as Mount Sinai. And on Sinai the law was given, begetting into slavery, and from Mount Sinai the tablets, having been given, were carried into Israel, and having been moved many times from place to place, they were finally set up in Jerusalem. Because of this he added: and it corresponds to the present Jerusalem, and it is in slavery with its children. Where there is a promise of land, and possession and marriage and human things, slavery also follows; but where there is release from earthly cares and from bonds, and the citizenship is in the heavens, from that citizenship itself comes freedom. It is asked why, drawing people away from the law, he mentions sin. Because the law commanded to live luxuriously, and through this desire is provoked and, being uncontrollable, leads to sin. For this reason, whenever there was mention of the law, he also mentions sin. For also in the letter to the Romans, mentioning the law, he also introduced the correction through the Lord: for those who live according to the flesh cannot please God. And why was living luxuriously and eating permitted? Because abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress, if eating and drinking had not been granted to them; for the lawgiver knew that it is impossible for those living luxuriously to master pleasures. But for the time being he wished to train the mind, so that it might know what is good and what is evil and what is piety; for he foresaw that the one who would supply what was lacking to the law was going to come, I mean the not walking according to the flesh, as Paul says. He showed from this that many were spending inopportunely, providing for those who urged them to keep the law, but provided nothing for those proclaiming Paul's teaching. Therefore he says: the one who sows into his own flesh; for the one subject to the law lives in fleshly things. Therefore the one who provides for the one teaching these things sows into the flesh only. So that he might not be thought to champion uncircumcision and not circumcision, and might not give a pretext for slander to those who oppose, he most beautifully added the last thing, that neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but he said a new creation. About which elsewhere: if anyone is in Christ, new creation. If it is a new creation, he says, do not be under the law; for the one living according to the law lives in the world, but the one living in Christ has his citizenship in the heavens. Therefore the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'allegory' for Paul's enacted prophecy, not a figurative reading.
The glossary requires 'slavery' for δουλεία, contrasting with freedom.
The heavenly citizenship is the source of freedom; 'citizenship' preserves the political metaphor.
The glossary requires 'new creation' for καινὴ κτίσις.
The verb means indulgence in food and drink, which the law permitted; 'live luxuriously' captures the bodily indulgence.

pass_b_english: So now he called the prophecy enacted through deeds an allegory. He did not mention Mount Sinai without reason, but because the Hagarenes, the descendants of Ishmael, hold the desert that stretches as far as Mount Sinai. On Sinai the law was given, and it gives birth into slavery. From Mount Sinai the tablets were given and carried into Israel, and after being moved many times from place to place they were finally established in Jerusalem. For this reason he added: she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, and she is in slavery with her children (Galatians 4:25). Where there is an earthly promise, and property, and marriage, and human affairs, slavery follows as well. But where there is release from earthly cares and from bonds, and citizenship is in heaven, freedom comes from that very citizenship.

The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin. It is because the law commanded eating, and through this desire is provoked, and since it is uncontrollable it leads to sin. For this reason, whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin. Indeed, in the letter to the Romans, when he mentions the law he also brings in the correction through the Lord: those who live according to the flesh cannot please God (Romans 8:8). But why was feasting and eating permitted? Because progress in abstaining from acknowledged evils would not have occurred unless eating and drinking had been permitted to them. For the lawgiver knew that it is impossible for those who feast to master their pleasures. For the time being, however, he wanted to train the mind, so that it might know what is good and what is evil and what is godly. For the lawgiver foresaw that Christ was going to come, who would supply what was lacking in the law—I mean not walking according to the flesh, as Paul says.

Eusebius explains that Paul made clear from this that many people were acting at the wrong time, providing for those who urged them to keep the law, but giving nothing to those who proclaimed Paul's teaching. Therefore he says: the one who sows to his own flesh. For the person subject to the law lives in fleshly things. Thus the one who gives to the one who teaches these things sows only into the flesh.

So that Paul might not be thought to be advocating uncircumcision and not circumcision, and so that he might not give a pretext for slander to his opponents, he added the final point most beautifully: neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but he said new creation. About this he says elsewhere (2 Corinthians 5:17): if anyone is in Christ, new creation. If it is a new creation, he says, do not come under the law. For the one living according to the law lives in the world, but the one living in Christ has citizenship in heaven. So the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Galatians 6:14).

problems.quote: the law permitted living luxuriously
problems.why: The Greek verb κελεύω means 'commanded' or 'ordered', not 'permitted'. The law commanded luxury, which provoked desire.
problems.fix: It is because the law commanded living luxuriously, and through this desire is provoked...
problems.ruling: Greek ἐκέλευεν = 'commanded', not 'permitted'; changes law’s role.

problems.quote: The question is raised why, when he is pulling people away from the law, he mentions sin.
problems.source_quote: Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
problems.why: Greek says the law itself remembers sin; English attributes the action to “he” and adds “pulling people away”.
problems.fix: The question is raised why the law, when removed, still remembers sin.
problems.ruling: νόμου ἀποσπῶν: law pulls away; μέμνηται: law remembers. English wrongly makes 'he' the agent.

problems.quote: For this reason, whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin.
problems.source_quote: τοῦτο ἕνεκεν ὅτε νόμου ἦν μνήμη, μέμνηται καὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
problems.why: Greek attributes the remembering of sin to the law, not to “he”.
problems.fix: For this reason, whenever the law is mentioned, it also remembers sin.
problems.ruling: νόμου ἦν μνήμη: 'law's memory/remembrance'; μέμνηται: law remembers. English wrongly adds 'he'.

problems.quote: So the one who provides for the teacher of these things sows only into the flesh.
problems.source_quote: ὁ τοίνυν τῷ ταῦτα διδάσκοντι παρέχων εἰς τὴν σάρκα σπείρει μόνον.
problems.why: Greek says the teacher himself (the one who teaches these) sows only into the flesh; English shifts the subject to the one who provides for the teacher.
problems.fix: Thus the one who teaches these things, giving support to the flesh, sows only into the flesh.
problems.ruling: ὁ...παρέχων: 'the one providing' is subject; τῷ...διδάσκοντι: dative 'to the teacher'. English inverts subject and recipient.

edits.new: It is because the law commanded living luxuriously

fixed: Changed 'permitted' to 'commanded' for κελεύω.
Corrected agency: the law itself remembers sin, not 'he'.

Corrected subject: the teacher himself sows into the flesh, not the one providing for him.

problems.quote: So that he might not be thought to be taking the side of uncircumcision rather than circumcision
problems.source_quote: Ἵνα μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκροβυστίας ἀντιποιεῖσθαι, καὶ οὐχὶ περιτομῆς …
problems.why: Reverses who is being favored; Greek says he does not want to be seen as opposing uncircumcision (i.e., favoring circumcision).
problems.fix: So that he might not be thought to be opposing uncircumcision (i.e., favoring circumcision) and not give his opponents a pretext for slander.

problems.quote: living luxuriously
problems.why: τρυφᾶν means 'to live delicately/luxuriously' but context shows law commanded feasting/celebration, not luxury; 'feasting' better.
problems.fix: feasting

problems.quote: luxurious living and eating
problems.why: Same error: τρυφᾶν is not 'luxurious living' but feasting/celebrating; 'eating and drinking' pattern follows.
problems.fix: feasting and eating
problems.ruling: τὸ τρυφᾶν καὶ ἐσθίειν = feasting and eating, not luxury

problems.quote: those who live luxuriously
problems.why: Same error repeated; lawgiver knew those who feast cannot control pleasures, not 'live luxuriously'.
problems.fix: those who feast
problems.ruling: τρυφῶντας = those who feast/indulge, not 'live luxuriously'

problems.quote: the one who teaches these things, giving support to the flesh
problems.source_quote: ὁ τοίνυν τῷ ταῦτα διδάσκοντι παρέχων
problems.why: Misread syntax: 'the one giving to the one who teaches these things'—the supporter, not the teacher, sows to flesh.
problems.fix: the one who gives to the one who teaches these things
problems.ruling: Greek says giver to teacher, translation flips roles

fixed: Agency: Greek ἀντιποιεῖσθαι with genitive means 'to champion/defend' something, so ἀκροβυστίας ἀντιποιεῖσθαι means 'to champion uncircumcision'; the English 'taking the side of uncircumcision rather than circumcision' reversed the meaning. Changed to 'opposing uncircumcision rather than circumcision' to match the source.
Mistranslation: τρυφᾶν means 'to live delicately/luxuriously' but in context the law commanded feasting/celebration; changed 'living luxuriously' to 'feasting'.
Mistranslation: Same τρυφᾶν issue; changed 'luxurious living and eating' to 'feasting and eating'.
Mistranslation: Same τρυφᾶν issue; changed 'those who live luxuriously' to 'those who feast'.

Mistranslation: Greek ὁ τῷ ταῦτα διδάσκοντι παρέχων means 'the one who gives to the one who teaches these things'; the English misread the syntax. Changed to 'the one who gives to the one who teaches these things'.

problems.quote: it still remembers sin
problems.why: Subject is Paul/author, not 'it' (the law). 'He remembers sin' or 'he mentions sin'.
problems.fix: he still mentions sin
problems.ruling: Greek subject is implied author, not 'it' (law)

problems.quote: it also remembers sin
problems.why: Same error: subject is Paul, not 'it'. 'He also mentions sin'.
problems.fix: he also mentions sin

problems.quote: whenever the law is mentioned, it also remembers sin

problems.fix: whenever there was mention of the law, he also mentioned sin

problems.quote: Romans 8:8
problems.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶντες θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται
problems.why: The quotation matches Romans 8:8, but Eusebius says 'in the letter to the Romans' without chapter reference. The translator added 'Romans 8:8'—but is this correct? The verse is Romans 8:8. However, the brief says 'Modern citations should use standard English Bible names'—but the source doesn't give chapter/verse. Adding a specific verse number is an addition not in source. Actually, checking: the source has 'Gal 4,25', 'Gal 5,17', 'Gal 6,7–8', 'Gal 6,14–15' explicitly. For Romans, it just says 'ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους'. The translator added '(Romans 8:8)'—this is an addition of specific reference not in source.
problems.fix: in the letter to the Romans
problems.ruling: Translator adds specific Romans 8:8 not in source

problems.quote: So that he might not be thought to be opposing uncircumcision rather than circumcision
problems.source_quote: Ἵνα μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκροβυστίας ἀντιποιεῖσθαι, καὶ οὐχὶ περιτομῆς
problems.why: ἀντιποιεῖσθαι means 'to lay claim to, contend for, be devoted to'—not 'opposing'. 'So that he might not be thought to be advocating uncircumcision and not circumcision'. The sense is reversed: Paul doesn't want to seem to be championing uncircumcision over circumcision.
problems.fix: So that he might not be thought to be advocating uncircumcision and not circumcision

problems.quote: 2 Corinthians 5:17
problems.source_quote: εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
problems.why: The source does not specify the book for this quotation. Eusebius says 'περὶ ἧς ἀλλαχοῦ' ('about which elsewhere'). The translator added '(2 Corinthians 5:17)'. This is an addition of specific reference not in the source text. The brief says modern citations should use standard English Bible names, but this applies when the source gives a reference. Here the source only says 'elsewhere'. Adding 2 Corinthians 5:17 is an addition.
problems.fix: About this he says elsewhere: if anyone is in Christ, new creation.
problems.ruling: Adds 2 Cor 5:17 not indicated in source

problems.quote: many people were spending at the wrong time, providing for those who urged them to keep the law
problems.source_quote: πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνέλησικον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελεύομενις
problems.why: Greek says many were acting untimely or improperly, urging those who keep the law; English adds “spending” which is not in the source.
problems.fix: many acted untimely, urging those who keep the law, while giving nothing to those who proclaim Paul’s teaching
problems.ruling: ἀνήλισκον means 'spending' but ἀκαίρως modifies it as 'untimely/improperly'; English inverts sense to 'spending at wrong time' rather than 'untimely they were spending'.

fixed: Changed 'it still remembers sin' to 'he still mentions sin' because the subject of μέμνηται is Paul/author, not the law.

problems.quote: the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked
problems.why: 'Feasting' is opposite of law's typical association with fasting/restriction; likely means 'festivals' or 'food laws.'
problems.fix: Revise to 'festivals' or clarify 'food regulations.'

problems.quote: the one who sows into his own flesh
problems.why: Galatians 6:8 has 'sows to the flesh' (metaphorical), but 'into his own flesh' sounds anatomically bizarre.
problems.fix: Revise to 'sows to his own flesh' or 'sows to the flesh.'

problems.quote: if anyone is in Christ, new creation
problems.why: Cited as 'elsewhere' but this is 2 Corinthians 5:17, not Galatians; Eusebius says 'elsewhere' correctly, but reader may expect Galatians citation.
problems.fix: Add citation: 2 Corinthians 5:17.

problems.quote: the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked
problems.why: 'Feasting' seems odd; Paul's argument about law provoking sin (Romans 7) usually concerns commandments provoking sinful desire, not feasting.
problems.fix: Check Greek; likely 'eating' or 'partaking' rather than 'feasting'—the law's food rules provoked desire.

problems.quote: Because abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress unless eating and drinking had been granted to them.
problems.why: Logic is unclear: why would abstaining from evils require permission to eat and drink? Seems to conflate dietary laws with moral law.
problems.fix: Likely means: 'They could not have progressed from known evils unless permitted some bodily indulgences.'

problems.quote: the one who sows into his own flesh. For the person subject to the law lives in fleshly things.
problems.why: First sentence is Paul's phrase but unmarked; second is Eusebius's explanation, but the transition is invisible.
problems.fix: Mark: 'Paul says: the one who sows into his own flesh. Eusebius explains: For the person subject to the law…'

problems.quote: About this he says elsewhere: if anyone is in Christ, new creation.
problems.why: This is 2 Corinthians 5:17, but no reference is given and 'elsewhere' is vague; a reader cannot locate it.
problems.fix: Add reference: 'About this he says elsewhere (2 Cor. 5:17): if anyone is in Christ, new creation.'

problems.quote: the circumcision party
problems.why: Same group (Jewish-observance advocates opposing Paul) is named differently each time without signal.
problems.fix: Use 'the circumcision party' consistently or signal equivalence on first variation.

fixed: The Greek τρυφᾶν means 'to live luxuriously' or 'to feast,' and the context contrasts it with abstinence from evils; 'feasting' is acceptable, though 'festivals' is not supported by the source. No change.
The Greek εἰς τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ means 'into his own flesh'; 'to his own flesh' is a more natural English rendering of the metaphor and matches Galatians 6:8.
The source says ἀλλαχοῦ ('elsewhere'), and the quotation is from 2 Corinthians 5:17; adding the citation helps the reader locate it.

The Greek ἀποχὴ τῶν ὡμολογημένων κακῶν means 'abstinence from acknowledged evils'; the logic is that without the concession of eating and drinking, they would not have progressed in abstaining from evils. The English is accurate.

The first sentence is Paul's quotation introduced by φησίν, and the second is Eusebius's explanation; the English already marks the quotation with 'he says' and the explanation follows naturally. No change needed.

problems.quote: the law
problems.why: Eusebius distinguishes 'commandments' (hearable, justifying) from 'works of the law' (bodily, toilsome), but this distinction is blurred by inconsistent rendering.
problems.fix: Clarify Eusebius's distinction between 'hearing commandments' and 'bodily works'.

problems.quote: basic principles
problems.why: Greek στοιχεῖα ('elements/basic principles') refers to elemental spirits or elementary teachings; 'basic principles' is opaque and its connection to law unclear.
problems.fix: Gloss as 'elemental spirits/powers' or explain equivalence to law.

problems.quote: the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked
problems.why: Opposite of expected: Jewish law restricts feasting (fast days, kosher laws). 'Feasting' likely mistranslates Greek for 'eating' or 'dietary laws'.
problems.fix: Use 'eating' or 'dietary regulations' instead of 'feasting'.

problems.quote: abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress unless eating and drinking had been granted to them
problems.why: Paradoxical: why must 'eating and drinking be granted' for abstinence to progress? 'Granted' likely means 'regulated' or 'permitted under restriction'.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'unless eating and drinking were first regulated'.

problems.quote: the one who sows to his own flesh. For the person subject to the law lives in fleshly things
problems.why: In Galatians 6:8, 'sow to the flesh' means gratifying sinful nature; Eusebius redefines it as supporting Torah-observant teachers, which stretches Paul's meaning.
problems.fix: Note Eusebius's interpretive move: 'Eusebius reads "flesh" here as Torah-observance'.

problems.quote: those who live according to the flesh cannot please God
problems.why: Attributed to 'the letter to the Romans,' but exact phrase is Romans 8:8. However, Eusebius introduces it to explain why Paul mentions sin with law, which is not Romans 8's context.
problems.fix: Correct reference to Romans 8:8; note Eusebius's application is thematic, not contextual.

problems.quote: The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin.
problems.why: Reader cannot tell who raises the question—an imagined objector, Eusebius himself, or a standard scholastic formula.
problems.fix: Mark as Eusebius's own question: 'Eusebius raises the question…'

problems.quote: For he foresaw that the one was going to come who would supply what was lacking in the law—I mean not walking according to the flesh, as Paul says.
problems.why: 'I mean' is Eusebius, 'as Paul says' introduces Paul, but the sentence structure makes the referent of 'the one' unclear (Christ? a future figure?).
problems.fix: Clarify: 'For the lawgiver foresaw that Christ was going to come…'

problems.quote: Because abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress unless eating and drinking had been granted to them.
problems.why: 'Abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress' is awkward; the meaning seems to be that progress could not occur without permitting eating/drinking.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'Because progress in abstaining from acknowledged evils would not have occurred unless eating and drinking had been permitted.'

problems.quote: those who live according to the flesh cannot please God
problems.why: The text says this is from 'the letter to the Romans' but does not give a reference; it is Romans 8:8. More importantly, Eusebius calls it a 'correction through the Lord,' but the words are Paul's, not the Lord's spoken words.
problems.fix: Add reference '(Romans 8:8)' and clarify that Paul, not the Lord directly, spoke these words.

problems.quote: He made clear from this that many people were acting at the wrong time, providing for those who urged them to keep the law, but giving nothing to those who proclaimed Paul's teaching.
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if 'He' is Paul or Eusebius; the sentence is Eusebius's commentary but the subject is ambiguous.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Eusebius explains that Paul made clear from this…'

problems.quote: So that he might not be thought to be advocating uncircumcision and not circumcision, and so that he might not give a pretext for slander to his opponents, he added the final point most beautifully
problems.why: 'He' is Paul but the sentence is Eusebius's commentary; the shift from previous section's 'I' to 'he' is unmarked.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'So that Paul might not be thought…'

fixed: The source says τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν ὁ νόμος, which means 'the law commanded to live luxuriously' or 'to feast'; 'feasting' is not a mistranslation of the Greek, but the confirmed problem says it is opposite of expected. The source clearly says the law commanded τρυφᾶν, so 'feasting' is accurate; however, the problem insists on 'eating' or 'dietary regulations'. The Greek τρυφᾶν means 'to live luxuriously, to feast', not simply 'to eat'. I will not change it because the source supports 'feasting'.

The source says ἀποχὴ οὐκ ἂν προεχώρησεν, εἰ μὴ ἐνεδόθη αὐτοῖς τὸ ἐσθίειν καὶ πίνειν. The English 'abstinence from acknowledged evils would not have made progress unless eating and drinking had been granted to them' is a literal rendering. The problem suggests 'progress in abstaining...' which is clearer. I made the edit to improve clarity.

The source says προεώρα γὰρ ὅτι ἔμελλεν ἔρχεσθαι ὁ τὸ λεῖπον τῷ νόμῳ προστιθείς. The English 'the one was going to come who would supply what was lacking in the law' is accurate but ambiguous. The problem suggests clarifying 'Christ'. The source does not name Christ, but the context implies it. I added 'Christ' for clarity.

The source says Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον. The English 'He made clear from this' is ambiguous. The problem suggests clarifying 'Eusebius explains that Paul made clear'. I made the edit.
The source says Ἵνα μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκροβυστίας ἀντιποιεῖσθαι. The English 'So that he might not be thought' is ambiguous. The problem suggests clarifying 'Paul'. I made the edit.

The source says τὸ οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶντες θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται. The English 'those who live according to the flesh cannot please God' is accurate. The problem suggests adding the reference Romans 8:8. I added the reference.
The problem about 'the law' glossary is not an edit to the English text but a glossary issue. The glossary already defines 'the law' as the Mosaic law with bodily observances. No edit needed.

The problem about 'basic principles' glossary is not an edit to the English text but a glossary issue. The glossary already defines 'basic principles' as the weak and poor elements of the world. No edit needed.
The problem about 'the one who sows to his own flesh' is not a mistranslation; the source says ὁ σπείρων εἰς τὴν σάρκα αὐτοῦ. The English is accurate. No edit needed.

The problem about 'The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin' is not a mistranslation; the source says Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας. The English is accurate. No edit needed.

dismissed.quote: why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin
dismissed.why: Greek says the law itself is remembered together with sin; English shifts agency to the author mentioning sin.
dismissed.note: The subject of μέμνηται is Paul, so 'he mentions sin' is right, and the proposed 'law is remembered' misreads the Greek.

dismissed.quote: But why was feasting and eating permitted?
dismissed.why: Again, τρυφᾶν means 'indulgence' or 'luxury', not 'feasting'. The context is about restraining pleasure.
dismissed.note: Here τρυφᾶν goes with the law's festal eating and drinking, so 'feasting' is a fair rendering.
